speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
May I inquire of the Prime Minister as to the accuracy of a statement which appears in The Financial Post of June 25, with respect to an important matter of government policy. It is, the report says, "from our own correspondent", Ottawa, and reads in part:
It was learned here officially that when Mr. Bennett made this announcement no definite policy had been worked out. Upon closer study, the difficulties of contributing 5 cents per bushel only to export wheat were disclosed. The government, faced by these difficulties, have abandoned the policy of a freight rate subvention on export wheat, and, instead, propose to bonus all wheat marketing by farmers, whether for export or for domestic consumption, by 5 cents per bushel. Just how the policy will be applied remains to be decided.
I should like to ask, first, whether the statement is a correct one, and secondly, in the event of its being correct, whether my right hon. friend does not feel that an important announcement of this kind should be made in the first instance to parliament.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I wholly agree with the view expressed in the last observation of the right hon. gentleman, that it would be highly improper to make a declaration of policy, in the first instance, elsewhere than in parliament when it is in session. I have endeavoured, so far as it has been within my power, strictly to adhere to that rule, bearing in mind that on many occasions I have heard the right hon. gentleman refer to the rule- a rule with respect to which, as I have often
said to him, I am wholly in accord with his views. No such statement was, to my knowledge, made to the correspondent of any newspaper, officially or otherwise, and I am sure that the right hon. gentleman would be the last to seek to hold any government accountable for what appears in the public press with respect to policies of governments. For if it were so, the policy of the late government would have been very much like that of its predecessor, and the policy of the present administration would probably be no policy at all. I can only say that the policy of this administration with respect to the matter in question will, of course, be made known in the measures founded upon the resolutions to be submitted to the house in due course.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: In answer to a question yesterday my right hon. friend intimated that, before the close of the day, he might have a statement to make with regard to the Australian treaty. Possibly that statement was inadvertently made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. I had expected a cablegram
before eleven o'clock. I looked into the matter after my right hon. friend had left last evening, and the position is this. A trade agreement has been signed between Australia and Canada. Duplicate copies were prepared. The copy signed here was mailed on the date of execution. The copy signed in Australia was mailed from that dominion, I believe, the next day after it was executed. In the ordinary passage of mails, it is not expected that the copy that left here will reach Australia before July 5, and the copy mailed from Australia will probably not reach here until July 7, as it is coming by way of 'San Francisco, there being no direct mail that could be utilized advantageously at that time. The government of Australia desires that statements with respect to the agreement be made simultaneously, and we have agreed to that view. As soon as they receive the copy signed here, they will immediately communicate with us. and when we receive their copy we shall at once communicate with them; and at the earliest possible moment thereafter a statement will be made on the same day to the parliament of Australia and to this house. One would hesitate to express a precise opinion with respect to the matter, but I should say that somewhere between the 7th
Trade with Australia

and the 9th-that is, either on the 8th or on the 9th-we should be able to make a state* ment here, as it is clear that the agreement will reach Australia prior to the date on which their copy will reach us. There should therefore be no delay after our receipt of the copy signed in Australia.

I do not want the Prime
Minister to disclose prematurely any matter of policy, but in connection with the Australian treaty, I noticed the other day, in a press despatch from Reuters, a statement made by the Prime Minister of New Zealand to the effect that they were prepared to negotiate a treaty with Canada but that no steps had been taken by the Canadian government. Will the Prime Minister say whether that is the case and, if so, whether steps might not be taken to arrange such a trade agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know whether
I should speak without referring to the documents, but I might say for the information of the house that, I think, my first experience of the administration of public affairs was the receipt from New Zealand of a message which was directed to the Prime Minister-and at the time it was sent that would have meant my right hon. friend opposite-in which that dominion veiy strenuously objected to the repeal of the agreement under which their butter came into our market at a cent per pound. And certain steps were then taken by the parliament of New Zealand to make it less easy for Canadian goods to find access to their markets. When the tariff was subsequently raised, the matter was discussed with the Prime Minister of New Zealand and his party as they passed through Canada, and later in England, but for some strange reason the Prime Minister of New Zealand represents the view of his government as being exactly as indicated by the newspapers: we must provide a market for their butter.

They will negotiate
on no other basis?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry to say that
just what Mr. Forbes said to the newspaper Correspondents was practically said to us, and that must be faced. The government sought recently some negotiation with the government of New Zealand looking towards a possible discussion of the whole matter, and it was suggested that one of our ministers should go to New Zealand. It was said that that would be very useful for many. reasons, and would be a friendly act on our part; that they had frequently come to our country but none of our ministers had been there. We were unable to give them any assurance 
in that regard. Influential bodies such as boards of trade and chambers of commerce have been interesting themselves in th>
matter, but in every instance there seems to be some difficulty with regard to butter. Whether or not any member of the government may be able to take that pleasant trip to New Zealand is a matter still under consideration; certain it is that at least one or two members will not be able to do so.

My right hon. friend has referred to a telegram which he has received from New Zealand in reply to one which was sent by the previous administration. He did not inform the house that in that telegram from Canada to New Zealand, to which the one he received was in reply, an arrangement was made whereby the duty against New Zealand butter would be four cents per pound pending the time when there might be a revision of the agreement, and it was suggested that that revision might be made when the Prime Minister of New Zealand was on his way to the Imperial conference provided he would come by way of Canada. That I understand was acceptable and the Premier of New Zealand came by way of Canada but on the day he arrived in Ottawa and began to negotiate with my right hon. friend, the government of the day, the present administration, raised the duty from four to eight cents per pound and the Premier of New Zealand a few days ago in advising his own parliament of the matter said that Mr. Bennett had slammed the door in his face the day he arrived at Ottawa and for that reason it was impossible to effect any further negotiation, and for that reason there was no alternative but to have the rate of the New Zealand general tariff made applicable to Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the
right hon. gentleman's recollection is entirely accurate, but I will satisfy myself upon that point and make a statement to the house. As to raising the duty to eight cents a pound, we did take that action and we did it because we believed we owed a duty to Canadian butter producers which was greater than any duty we owed to the butter producers of any other part of the world.

Hon, H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, in regard to the last return to which my hon. friend refers, I would state that that return called for the typing of over two hundred pages, not only of correspondence but of statements containing technical matter and figures of a very complicated character. I thank my hon. friend for that, but there are other returns which I have not received and which could be answered in half an hour.

(Minister of Trade and Commerce): I shall make inquiries.

If not, I shall be in a position to make another motion to get it. I am very sorry the minister did not comply with the order of the house.

The return was prepared by the officials of my department and my instructions were that they should put into that return the whole correspondence. I shall inquire further to see whether there are other letters. If there are, I shall have no objection whatever to laying them before the house.
I thank the minister, but he made the statement himself.

Will the Minister of Marine be kind enough to instruct his officers to comply with an order of a return placed on the order paper the first day of the session, which order was passed very early in the month of March. Would he instruct his officers to expedite the matter?

I shall inquire again and I hope I shall be able to give an answer to the house to-morrow. I do not know why the return was not brought down sooner. Of course the matter was overlooked by me, but I am sure the return will be forthcoming soon.

A similar question might be addressed to the Minister of National Defence, except that the order for return was passed perhaps a month later, with respect to correspondence dealing with the Ross Rifle Company.

speechtext:
The correspondence

Dominion Wheat Board
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, a headline appears in
the Financial Post of June 25 which states: "Wheat board is not likely, Ottawa hears.'' In view of the fact that the three western provinces have been stressing to the government the necessity of the establishment of a wheat board, and also because of the fact that many of the western members are receiving resolutions regarding this matter, I would like to ask the government if it is now in a position to state whether the farmers can expect the establishment this year of a wheat board.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman
knows perfectly well that representatives of the western provinces were here yesterday and made their representations to the government, and that no conclusion was arrived at. The matter is under consideration and it affords me an opportunity to point out to my fellow western members that the question of the creation of a wheat board is now surrounded with legal difficulties in consequence of the decisions of the court of last resort of our empire, to which the attention of the house well might be directed. As I pointed out yesterday to the legal representatives of the provinces, these decisions in connection with the commerce and news print cases were to the effect that it was not competent for the Dominion to infringe upon the semi-sovereign rights-I think that is the language of Lord Haldane-of the provinces by endeavouring, for instance, to fix the prices of commodities or deal with matters of that character; that property and civil rights were solely within the jurisdiction of the provinces and could not be taken away from them by any act of the parliament of Canada unless a national emergency such as war existed. If my hon. friend cares to pursue further his study he will find that in the later case, in connection with the fixing of the price of newsprint, the matter was discussed further. Whether or not the Dominion parliament could pass any statute which would enable a board created by it to carry on business and function as a private trader representing the government is a matter not free from doubt. I suggested to the gentlemen another method by which the ends aimed at might be accomplished, and that matter is under their consideration as it is under ours. I am sure that if the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to consult with those who have had to give much fMr Sutherland.]
study and thought to this matter, if he will take into consideration the decisions of the courts fixing clearly the jurisdiction of this parliament in times of peace, on the one hand, as distinguished from the jurisdiction of the provinces in times of peace, on the other hand, he will realize that the creation of such an organization as he suggests entails more than the mere mentioning of it.

Could not
the constitutional difficulties to which the Prime Minister has referred be obviated by the provinces passing concurrent legislation validating the federal act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The privy council is very clear about that. The question of validating a dominion act by provincial statute, it is hardly necessary to say, is something not possible of accomplishment. Provincial legislation cannot validate dominion legislation. Dominion legislation either lies within or without the ambit of the powers of parliament; provincial legislation either lies within or without the legislative jurisdiction of the province. If without, no action on our part can give it validity; if within, it requires no action to give it validity. It is hardly necessary to say that in the case in connection with the peaceful settlement of strikes and disputes between employers and employees the provinces passed legislation which had been declared by the dominion to be ultra vires of the dominion; it being ultra vires of the dominion, it was, of course, intra vires of the provinces. It does not follow that the mere passing of legislation which is ultra vires of the dominion will in itself give the dominion powers even if the provinces ask that those powers be accepted. That is the real position with respect to the matter. But without an analysis of it in that sense, the discussion proceeded upon suggestions that were made for the purpose of endeavouring to see whether some method might not be devised that would accomplish the purpose aimed at without contravening any fixed legal principles. It is, I presume, unnecessary to say that there is a large body of public opinion that does not approve of a wheat board, and any single individual would have the right to resort to the courts for the purpose of testing the validity of any legislation that might be enacted. He would be entitled to an injunction just as any litigant might be. Therefore it is of paramount importance that the matter, when dealt with, shall be dealt with in some manner that will not invite litigation nor contravene any fixed legal principle that we know governs in the administration of our constitutional rights.

Together with the final protocol,

at London on the 31st day of May, 1929 (in this act referred to as the safety convention), and set out in schedule I to this act, and the convention, known as the international convention respecting load lines, together with the final protocol, signed at London on the 5th day of July, 1930 (in this act referred to as the load line convention), and set out in schedule II to this act, are hereby confirmed and sanctioned, and the provisions of the said conventions shall have the force of law.

speechtext: My hon. friend cannot move an amendment to his own bill. If should be moved by one of his colleagues.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: I move the amendment, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: Will the minister be good enough to explain just what this means. What is meant by the load line?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext:
This bill, as indicated by the title, and as provided for specifically by section 2, has for its object the ratification of twio international conventions respecting shipping. One of these, set out in schedule one of the act is the international convention for the safety of life at sea, which was signed at London on May 31, 1929. The other is the international load line convention, which was signed at London on July 5, 1980. The first convention becomes effective as from July 1, 1931, provided that the requisite number of ratifications have been effected before that date. The other convention does not become effective until on or after July 1, 1932.
It will be useful at this point to refer briefly to the steps that led up to the conclusion of these two conventions. I shall deal first with the convention for the safety of life at sea. It will doubtless be within the recollection of many hon. members of this house that following the disaster to the steamship Titanic in the month of April, 1912, there was a general awakening on the part of all nations in the interests of humanity to the necessity of examining with the greatest care and thoroughness the possibility of strengthening the measures then existing providing for the safety of life at sea. All the nations came to the conclusion that there should be a convention to study this question as well as the question of load lines. The first convention was held in 1929, and the other in 1930.	.
The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysbor-ough has asked what a load line is. I suppose it is the depth of the load that can be put into a boat, and that load line must be marked on the side of the ship. The loads differ in different zones.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: I always thought that the loads were in ships' holds, not in different zones. Might I ask what the load line had to do with the loss of the Titanic?

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: All the nations were awakened by that disaster to the necessity of providing for the safety of life at sea, and that is why the convention was held in 1929. The load line question was also dealt with at that first convention, which had to do with the protection of the life of passengers and of the crews on ships.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: Does the minister mean to say that in the case of passenger ships the load line determines how many passengers shall be carried.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: I do not say that. I say that the convention of 1929 dealt with the protection of life at sea, particularly of life on passenger ships, but it also dealt with the load line in merchant vessels, for these vessels also carry passengers and crew as well as cargoes, as I suppose the hon. gentleman knows.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: I do not think the minister has given quite an accurate explanation of the load line. The load line as adopted by the convention is based on the old Board of Trade rules of 1906 in Great Britain, which make it compulsory to put on the side of a ship a disc, the centre of the disc indicating the line to which the ship may be loaded in the summer, and roughly six inches below that mark being the load line for the winter months.

Section as amended agreed to.

Ships when engaged on international voyages between the near neighbouring ports of two or more countries may be exempted by the administration to which such ships belong from the provisions of this convention, so long as they shall remain in such trades, if the governments of the countries in which such ports are situated shall be satisfied that the sheltered nature and conditions of such voyages between such ports make it unreasonable or impracticable to apply the provisions of this convention to ships engaged in such trades.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I
be excused for intervening at this time for but a single moment. The bill before us is founded upon a convention that was agreed to in 1929 and which had to deal with the safety of life at sea. Under the international convention through which this agreement was arrived at the word "sea" excluded the inland lakes to which my hon. friend has referred. Therefore by the legislation now before us we could not bring such inland lakes within the terms of the agreement. At the moment we are only ratifying an international arrangement in connection with which the views of Canada were expressed, if my memory serves me correctly, by the Deputy Minister of Marine, Mr. Alexander Johnston, and by Mr. Lueien Pacaud, secretary in the office of the Canadian High Commissioner in London.
My hon. friend the member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff)-whom I sometimes designate as the admiral because of his knowledge of the high seas,-will realize that in this instance we could not deal with a subject which I agree with him is of great importance. Those of us who have followed the results of storms in the fall realize that death by misadventure on the lakes is very great. To deal with such a matter we would have to make it the subject of another convention altogether. If my hon. friend will do me the kindness to look at the words of the
preamble to the convention he will find the following:
.... being desirous of promoting safety of life at sea by establishing in common agreement uniform principles and rules directed thereto.
That is the reason that coastal waters and lakes are excluded from the word "sea".
Although the hon. member who referred to the load line is not now in the chamber may I say that the words to which he referred are of most interesting derivation. The line referred to is not usually described as the load line, but is usually termed the "Plimsoll mark." Samuel Plimsoll espoused the cause of humanity in the days when great shipowners sent out ships which were not seaworthy and which as a result of overloading were responsible for the loss of a great many lives. Through succeeding years of advocacy in the British House of Commons, Samuel Plimsoll was successful, through the Board of Trade, in establishing a load line, and his name and fame are now perpetuated by the use of the words "Plimsoll mark" upon that disc which carries marks, one for the winter season, another for the summer season, one for the north Atlantic and another for the south Atlantic. Anyone who wishes to inspect a ship in port will see the Plimsoll mark upon its side indicating the load mark or load line referred to in this convention.
Undoubtedly every hon. member on this side of the house at least would like to give effect to the very humanitarian suggestions of the hon. member, but the limitations imposed upon us are such that we can only reject or accept the convention; that is one of the prices we pay for conventions of all kinds. The international convention arrived at this agreement only after a tremendous amount of work, and I am sure if any hon. member will look at the list of names ait pages 6, 7, 8 and 9 of the schedule to the bill he will realize that the best men who could be secured from the various parts of the world attended for the purpose of endeavouring to arrive at satisfactory conclusions. For instance, hon. members will note that the German ambassador headed the delegation of that country. Australia was represented by naval men. Denmark, Spain and the Irish Free State were represented by men of high repute, and the United States of America was represented not only by distinguished diplomatic civilians but also by technical men of the first order. The same may be said of other governments of the world. I therefore suggest to the committee in no captious or critical spirit at all that we are very largely limited in the amendments we may be in a position to make to the legislation.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTIONS SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext:
I understand the amendment had nothing to do with the convention. I thank my hon. friend, however, for bringing that matter to the attention of the committee because had he not done so I had intended to do so myself. So far as the substantive body of the convention is concerned we must either accept or reject it. If we reject it we of course have repudiated the action of our own representative, and I am sure this house has no intention to take any such action.
I am told, and having looked at the bill [DOT]now before me, I am prone to believe that the convention represents a tremendous amount of hard work by the very foremost experts of the world. For instance, if hon. members care to turn to pages 46 and 47 of the schedule attached to the bill they will ascertain the methods by which certain calculations are made, and the formulae employed.
I am sure they will readily realize that in order to prepare such formulae a very thorough knowledge of higher mathematics is required. So that the convention did not deal only with the question of safety at sea. in the narrow sense of the term, but dealt with it in the broader sense of the term, and discussed many points which come within the realm of navigation. 1931; that is point number one. Should five countries signify their adherence to this convention before July 1, 1931, then it would be in force between those governments; then the other governments may come in by depositing their ratifications, and three months afterwards, as my hon. friend has said the convention becomes effective as between them and the rest of the countries which have signed. As my hon. friend, the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has said, ratification is the essence, and that is what we are doing. The formality of ratification is a technical matter but what we are doing is giving the approval of parliament to the convention so that formal ratification may follow thereafter. The formal ratification is the technical means by which we deposit in the archives at London our accession to the convention and our acceptance of it as governing our maritime activities.

This government is trying to help all the ports. In Halifax works are under construction which were started over two years ago and are not completed yet. There is a pier, for instance, which is not yet completed. We have to see that this pier and the sheds which were started a year ago are completed. All the money that we are asking to-day for Halifax is for the purpose of completing works which were started a year or two ago. In the city of Montreal all the work which has been started has been completed. During these last few months we have authorized work to complete certain sheds at Montreal and to build grain loaders costing many thousands of dollars. Halifax Harbour

do not say that Windmill point pier will not be built. I think it will be built within a very short time. Since tolls are to be collected I may be permitted to make some observations in that regard. In the years 1927, 1928 and 1929, when under a previous administration bills were placed before the house providing for loans to the ports of Halifax and St. John, the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister, contended that we were absolutely wrong in our policy in regard to the development of these ports, especially those of Halifax and St. John; that it should not be continued and that we should adopt instead a policy of free ports by which the dominion government would not lend money to these ports, but under a commission would regard the advance so made as a charge against the federal treasury. Referring to the Duncan report the present Prime Minister is reported at page 2564 of Hansard, third volume, 1929, as follows:
It was not intended that these ports should be regarded as commission ports in the sense

in which we ordinarily use that term, implying self-sustaining undertakings, but that they should be considered to be national ports out of which, summer and winter, goods might be exported in order that the idea which was behind the confederation of the maritime provinces and the other parts of the dominion should be carried out.
Then, in Hansard, of 1929, at page 2565, volume 3, I find the following:
The situation is one which if it continues cannot but be injurious to those ports, and must bring about a condition which will prevent the accomplishment of the purpose intended in the expenditure of the moneys in question.

I submit that the Duncan report did not contemplate that sort of national port development; it contemplated a direct expenditure of public money for the purpose of developing the ports of St. John and Halifax.
Again, on page 2388 of the same volume I find the following:
I cannot think that we are doing our duty by the ports of Halifax and St. John if we merely create harbour commissions under the conditions of the existing Harbour Commissions Act, and ask those bodies to issue securities at five per cent per annum and expect them to pay either the principal or the interest. We should make an appropriation of such money from year to year as is required for the purpose of developing those harbours, and it should be a charge upon the revenues of the Canadian people.
During the last election, as I pointed out the other day, the right hon. Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, speaking in St. John said:
The port of St. John should be a great free port, a national port, and towards the implementation of this object I give my pledge. It is said that I am opposed to the port of St. John as at present operated. I am opposed to the collection of tolls in this port which prevents it from being built up. My ambition is to see this port the cheapest in the world.
Now that the Prime Minister is in power, having laid down this policy on three occasions and having given this direct promise to the people of St. John and Halifax, I think it is about time for him to put that policy into operation. Instead of introducing a measure providing for a loan of 83,500,000 for Halifax, and a further loan of $3,500,000 for St. John, which I will discuss more fully at a later time, the Prime Minister should bring in legislation authorizing this government, under plans prepared and approved by the governor in council, to expend the money directly and not continue the practice which he so severely condemned when the Liberal party was in power.

We are continuing the work which was started or authorized by the

late government, and nothing else. If it is the desire of my hon. friends that this bill should stand, it will stand until another session, but they will get their answer from the people of Halifax.
I am not opposing this bill.

We have to finish those works, but we have asked Sir Alexander Gibb, an outstanding marine engineer, to study our national ports and report on the improvements which should be proceeded with during the next twenty-five or fifty years, and also on a plan of administration. This clearly indicates that the government is not satisfied with the way our national ports are administered. For the. time being, however, since the works are going on, we feel that they should be concluded. This house voted loans last year to these harbour commissions; contracts have been let in excess of the amounts voted at that time, and now that the works are going on they must have more money. These works were under way when we came into power, and now we are being criticized by hon. gentlemen opposite when we are only continuing their work and nothing else.
I think my hon. friend will realize that when we have the report of Sir Alexander Gibb the administration of these ports will change, and we hope that with time our national ports will become free ports. Of course these things cannot 'be done over night or even in a year or two. Every hon. gentleman knows that perfectly well. We are only continuing the work started by the late government; we are helping these ports, and that is all.
I understood the minister to say the dther day that he was asking for these loans in order to provide for works which had been started without proper authorization, as well as other works.

This money is required to finish the piers and sheds and the other work which was under way last year; it is to finish the unauthorized works, and also do put these piers and wharves into operation. There must be grain loaders and other facilities before the piers and wharves may be used.

It is quite true, and I never attempted to deny, that 'the government are carrying on the works which were started by the late government, but the very conditions which exist now existed at the time 'the right hon. Prime Minister made his pledge to Halifax and St. John. He knew what the conditions were, and when he made that election promise to those people he had no idea at

all that he would have to gelt Sir Alexander Gibb to come over here. This is just a blind to cover up a promise which the government do not intend to carry out. I think my hon. friend who has just sat down is perfectly right, that at the time that statement to which he has referred was made in this house the right hon. gentleman criticized us severely for putting in the form of a loan any advance to these harbour commissions. remarks with respect to those who are criticizing, not this bill, but the failure of the present government to carry out their promises. speechtext:
Carry? Like fun
it carries. If my hon. friend wishes a specific question concerning the Stamp report I would state that hon. members on this side of the house are curious to know how that famous chart or appendix No. 10 crept into the
Stamp commission report. I presume the chart appears merely as an accident, and of course accidents will happen even in the best regulated governments. We would like to know however the particulars in connection with the publication of the chart. If hon. members look at the report they will find several charts at the back of it, and I refer particularly to No. 10.

There is nothing mysterious about the chart. I understand that with the exception of the chart at the end of the report all other charts and appendices are official and form part of the report. Chart No. 10 purports to set forth the open market trading cash price versus the Saskatchewan pool net payment, basis Fort William. I understand chart No. 10 was prepared by Mr. William Sanford Evans who was a member of the commission.
Tabled by him?

Yes, tabled by him with the commission and inserted in the report without comment. I think I have laid before the committee all the facts concerning chart No. 10. Of course the information contained in the chart or what the chart purports to set forth is before the committee for whatever observations hon. members may choose to make.
The Prime Minister indicated his view in the matter by stating that if there were a reprint of the report this chart No. 10 would be eliminated.
Yes, if there were objections to it.
There are certainly many objections throughout the west.
That is conceded.

The question arises as to how the chart appeared in the report. If it is wrong to print the chart in the reprint surely it was just as wrong to print it in the original document. Surely a piece of propaganda such as chart No. 10 on behalf of the grain exchange and against the pool is most unfair. The pool is up against it sufficiently without everybody jumping on its neck at this time when, if ever, its friends should be behind it. If the government pretends to be a friend of the pool I think some explanation should be forthcoming as to how chart No. 10 happened to appear in the Stamp report. I have noticed that William Sanford Evans was around here for some days after the report was understood to be filed. I wonder if his sojourn around the par-

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
liament buildings and the city of Ottawa had anything to do with chart No. 10 appearing in the report.

I assure my hon. friend
most solemnly that his stay in the city had nothing to do with the appearance of the chart.
No?

May I reassure my hon.
friend that there is nothing mysterious about the chart. It was inserted when the report was compiled because it was with the papers tabled or filed with the commission. Further than that I have no personal knowledge of it whatsoever. So far as the physical effort of placing the chart in the report is concerned I should say it was inserted probably as an exhibit at the end of the report. I wish to state clearly however that there is no pretence that this chart is a portion of the official report. It is not commented upon, is not commended to anybody and no one is placing any deduction upon it.

I notice that Sir
Josiah Stamp was particularly fair with all parties during the investigation.
I thought so.

I think he was a
model chairman.
I thought so.

For those reasons
I cannot conceive for a moment that Sir Josiah Stamp would have consented to the insertion of a chart such as No. 10. I think he would be very much surprised and probably astounded if he were to learn that this scandalous chart appeared at the end of the report.

I do not think he had
anything to do with it.
No, I do not think he had.

May I ask the minister how the chart happens to appear in the report? Are all the commissioners responsible? Had they knowledge that the chart would be placed in the report, and if not, who was responsible for its appearance, and for what purpose was it inserted? Those are the questions the farmers of western Canada are asking.

I cannot add to what I
have already stated. For the third time may I say that there is nothing mysterious about 
the appearance of the chart. No one pretends that the chart is a part of the body of the report, and it is not referred to in the report.
Why is it there?

So far as I know Sir
Josiah Stamp did not authorize the placing of it there because I think the report was printed after he left the country. I do not think he saw the final proof or make-up of the report. The government does not seek in any way to defend the presence of the chart in the report, and without hesitancy we say if there is any objection the chart will not be included in any future copies. I think I can go no farther than that in the matter. The government had no knowledge that this chart was being inserted in the report.

It is all very well for
the minister to make a statement, but the farmers still want to know who is responsible for the placing of the chart in the report. The Stamp commission was set up by this government to do specific things. There appears attached to the commission's report a certain chart; can the minister tell us who printed it?

No, I do not know, and
I do not see any markings on the chart to show who printed it.

Well then, who supervised the printing of it, and who is responsible? The minister says he does not know who printed it and I want to know who is responsible for its appearance in the report. Certainly someone must be responsible. The government set up a commission to do specific things, and at the end of the report of the commission we find this chart. This report is now up for discussion by the parliament that gave the commission its powers. I think it. is only reasonable that those of us who have some interest in this whole investigation should know the facts. This thing was printed by somebody, somewhere. Somebody was responsible for placing it there, and surely the commission which made the report must have some knowledge as to how it got there. I should like to ask the minister to tell us.

I have already stated that so far as I know' the report was prepared by Mr. Sanford Evans, a member of the commission; was filed by him with the commission, and I am now7 hazarding a guess, which I think is reasonable, that with his authority it was put in the report, but that I do not know definitely. I assume that, and I think it is a fair assumption.

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
I suppose the government will assume the responsibility for having it placed here?
No.

Surely if you appoint
a commission and the commission reports, and the government accept that report, they must stand behind the commission which they created.

Is there no answer
to that?
There was no question involved.

I want to know if the
government are behind the report submitted by Sir Josiah Stamp, and whether this chart was attached to it when the government first received the report from Sir Josiah Stamp.

Absolutely yes; this report was received as it is, as I have it in my hand, with these charts attached. Furthermore, my hon. friend made three or four assumptions a moment ago; he assumed the government was behind this and behind that. The government appointed Sir Josiah Stamp to make a certain investigation, and we believe he earned out his work expeditiously, well, fairly and in justice to all concerned. We have had many encomiums passed upon his chairmanship. We received and accepted his report. As to whether the government is behind every word of that report is another matter with which I am not prepared to deal to-night. But this is a report submitted to the house by the government as received from Sir Josiah Stamp.
In reference to this chart which is complained of, we had no knowledge of how it got there or anything else until it was brought to my attention some time after the report was filed. I noticed that it was not referred to in the report, and upon inquiry I learned that the chart was prepared by Mr. Sanford Evans and filed with the commission or laid upon the table of the commission during some of its proceedings. Why it is in the report or why it was put in the report I do not know. It is quite open to anyone to criticize its presence there; we are not objecting to that, but, I think, I have made just as complete an explanation as I can make of the position of the government in this regard.

The minister himself
admits there is no reference in the report to this chart.
I do not admit it; I have stated it three times.
Was this chart presented to the commission as an exhibit? Was it submitted as evidence? Surely it could not have been, or it would have been referred to in the report, would it not?
Not necessarily.
Then will the minister say this chart was presented as evidence?

How can I say that? I
was not present at the meetings. My hon. friend must be reasonable.

I am reasonable, but
the farmers want to know how it got there.
Oh, oh.

It is all very well for
you fellows who do not want to get to the bottom of this-

May I repeat for the fourth time the position we take in regard to this matter. I understand the chart was prepared by Mr. Sanford Evans, a member of the commission, and was filed by him with the commission during the period of its sittings. I have gone through the report quite carefully, and I do not see that the chart is referred to. I am informed by others who have examined the report that it is their opinion also that it is not referred to. Therefore I make this assumption-and in this I may be doing an injustice to Mr. Evans-that when the report was completed Mr. Evans, thinking this chart might be of some value, had it attached to the report. Whether he was right or wrong in that is a question to be determined by those who are desirous of criticizing the chart, but upon the government discovering that it was not referred to in the report and obviously was not a part of the exhibits of the whole commission, we called in or stopped the further circulation of the report containing this chart. That is the position.
Then the report as tabled has not been accepted? Are we to assume that?

I do not know what my hon. friend means by "accepted." The report as presented by Sir Josiah Stamp has been received by the government and presented to parliament for its consideration. No action has been taken with regard to accepting or approving it; it is before parliament for what it may be worth. We think Sir Josiah Stamp discharged his duties in an exemplary manner.

It seems to me that if this chart is in the report with the knowledge of all the commissioners it is a part of the report

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
and the government have no right to eliminate it from any future publication. If it is not a part of the report with the knowledge of all the commissioners; if it is there only at the instance of Mr. Sanford Evans, without the consent of the other commissioners, it has no business being there at all. We ought to know the exact situation.

I should like to read a question asked the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke), which appears at page 2812 of Hansard:
I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that the farmers of Saskatchewan are somewhat concerned regarding appendix XII of the Stamp commission report which sets out comparative pool and open market prices covering the years 1924 to 1931, will the Prime Minister state whether the appendix referred to was included in the original report ?
Eight Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister): My attention has been drawn to the matter. As I understand it, the appendix was an exhibit filed with the commission ....
I suggest there is no evidence of that at all; I understand from the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this is not so.
What is my hon. friend saying?

I am quoting the language of the Prime Minister at page 2812 of Hansard, in which he says this was an exhibit filed with the commission. I deduced from the remarks of my hon. friend this evening that this is not so.

Let me again make myself clear. What I stated was that my understanding was that Mr. Sanford Evans, a member of the commission, prepared this chart and filed it with the commission, or laid it on the table. Whether or not it was an exhibit, and whether or not he accompanied it with any evidence, I do not know.

Of course it is obvious that it could not be an exhibit, because if it were an exhibit it would be referred to in the printed portion of the report. The chart, therefore, was placed there absolutely without any authorization from any source whatever. Let me continue the reply of the right hon. Prime Minister:
.... and it was to be included in the report of the commission, but there is upon that appendix some printing which draws inferences that may or may not have been warranted, and that should not have been there. The diagram itself is not a matter of great importance; the objectionable feature is the printing that was put on it, I think by the grain exchange ....
IMr. Young.]
Here we have a most unique and anomalous situation. A commission is appointed by this government to make an inquiry into certain very important matters affecting the farmers of the west. A report is presented to the government, and in turn the government presents that Teport to parliament. We find an essential portion of that report is a certain diagram containing certain printing which is absolutely erroneous in intent, I think, which in my opinion should not have been there and which the Prime Minister says should not have been there. I say, Mr. Chairman, that this report should be returned by parliament to the government and by the government back to the commission, and that Sir Josiah Stamp himself should be consulted in regard to how this mysterious document was permitted to appear on the pages of the report.

The reply of the Prime Minister means this: "Somebody is guilty of a great blunder, but we will not do it again as far as the government is concerned." That is what it means. Well, Mr. Chairman, as a member of this house and also as a .pool contract signer in a big institution that is in economic trouble, like many others, I want to know more about this matter than the minister has so far indicated. My next statement will be that, simultaneously with the appointment of thi3 Stamp commission, an inquiry was instituted in Winnipeg with one Mr. Williams presiding as commissioner. That has just terminated, and the report of that commission shows up very badly, so far as it goes, against the elevator system of the Manitoba pool. It looks to me like a simultaneous attack all along the line against the pool. Just about two or three weeks before the Stamp commission was appointed, newspaper reports, both east and west, indicated that there was going to be such a commission, and actually forecast not only the personnel of the commission but the verdict. They brazenly indicated what the verdict was going to be, even before the commission was appointed. Then when it appeared that the pool had trouble within its own ranks on the 100 per cent question, someone concluded that, in view of these internal difficulties, they would leave the pool to itself and confine the inquiry to a report on grain futures. But, Mr. Chairman, the answer to the question which was submitted to the commission was already known; it was contained in the Turgecm report. But my hon. friends had committed themselves to a commission of some kind, and not wishing to go ahead with a commission of wider scope,

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
such as they had been talking about, they decided to have a commission headed by a first class man, with two other admittedly capable men. And they narrowed the scope of the commission down to one question, as to what effect the selling of futures had upon producers, whether prejudicial or otherwise. Wliat a profound question that was to make all this fuss about. To think that a government, supposed to be composed of business men, possessed of all kinds of knowledge within its ranks, should seriously sit down and ask a capable commission such as this to inquire into one single question, a question the answer to which anyone who had any knowledge of business whatever knew before the question was asked, is hard to understand. Why, there is nothing so mysterious about grain futures. The Turgeon commission, among many other things, went into that question fully; and the Stamp commission was big enough to refer to the Turgeon commission's much similar report. Indeed, the results are practically the same except with respect to certain oscillations, as it is called, in the market, with regard to futures in abnormal times.
So that we have more than one count against my hon. friend. In the first place, we cannot understand why he should have appointed a commission of that nature to inquire into such a simple question, the answer to which they had themselves, under their hands, in the files which have been there for the last five or six years. The question of selling futures is a general one which does not apply to wheat alone. You cannot order a ticket from here to London without someone selling you future delivery of space or reservation. The same with goods: you buy summer goods by order in the spring. Yet this government seriously sat down and asked this question about futures-asked a commission of this character to investigate a question like that. The whole thing, in my estimation, was a thinly camouflaged attack on the wheat pools, and in the absence of a better explanation-

Why does
the hon. gentleman call it a camouflage?

I qualified it; I
said it was a thinly camouflaged attack, on the wheat pool, and the camouflage was indeed very thin. My hon. friend the minister will have to put up something better, or we shall all arrive at that conclusion, and so will the public.

There
are twelve appendices in this report. If the
committee will look through it they will find in each appendix a statement with reference to the chart accompanying it, giving information as to where and by whom the chart was submitted, and upon whose authority. In connection with appendix 12, there is a curious diagram with most perverse propaganda at the bottom of the page. It says, "The above chart represents," and there is not a single authority in the dominion who has assumed responsibility for either the diagram or the words printed beneath.

I would direct the
attention of the committee to the order of reference to the commission. I quote:
The committee of the Privy Council on the recommendation of the Right Honourable Richard Bedford Bennett, the Prime Minister, advise that
Sir Josiah Stamp, G.B.E.,
The Honourable J. T. Brown, Chief Justice. Court of King's Bench, Saskatchewan, and
William Sanford Evans, Esquire, Winnipeg, Manitoba, be appointed, under the provisions of part I of the Inquiries Act, a commission to inquire into and report upon what effect, if any, the dealing in grain futures has upon the price received by the producer.
Those hon. gentlemen who know the purpose for which the wheat pools were established will recall that in the first years of their operation they sold direct; they never dealt in futures. This commission was appointed to look into the effect of futures on the producer, and we find in the report an appendix that purports to set out the operations of those who are dealing in grain futures to the detriment of the cooperative movement. As has been stated, it is nothing but sheer propaganda against the cooperative system of marketing. The minister may say what he likes now about deleting this objectionable appendix, but does he know how many copies have already been distributed not only in Canada but beyond the confines of this dominion. Does the minister know how far it has gone?
It will be filed in every library in the country.

Chief
Justice Brown of Saskatchewan has already, in the public press, repudiated this very document which my hon. friend attributes to Mr. Sanford Evans. I do not know whether the government is going to pay Mr. Evans, but in the face of this gigantic blunder I suggest that he certainly should be deprived of remuneration for his services if he deliberately seeks to incorporate, in what is supposed to be an impartial report, absolutely perverse propaganda.

Supply-Royal Grain Commission

I entirely agree with the criticism of previous speakers in this connection. It is quite obvious that this additional appendix has been inserted for a purpose. It is one too many, and although the minister has said that it will be deleted, its deletion will take place too late; the damage is already done. The conclusion one is expected to draw from the printed words is that No. 3 pool wheat brought less on the average in every year of the operation of the pool than, No. 3 wheat sold by open market methods. No such conclusion can be properly drawn from the chart itself. There is no evidence to show the real volume of wheat sold at any given time and at what particular price. As a matter of fact, a close analysis of the market situation during the periods under review in this chart might readily indicate that the open market selling of wheat was less advantageous than the marketing through the pool during the same period. A chart of this kind is obviously prepared for propaganda purposes, purely and simply to discredit the pool organization, which is the fruit of the cooperative movement in western Canada. Knowingly or unknowingly, the government has been made a party to this propaganda. I do not know to what extent the responsibility is attributable to this administration, either through the Prime Minister or through the Department of Trade and Commerce. But certainly this part of the report should at once be repudiated by the government. If they do not repudiate it, they become a party to and accept the propaganda it carries.

I have stated at least four ;imes in the clearest language of which I am capable that we had nothing whatever to do with the insertion of this diagram in the report. The moment our attention was drawn to the fact that it was obviously not part of the report we stopped the further distribution of the report and ordered that no more copies should be sent out containing this diagram. We have made inquiry and the full explanation is, as I have stated four times, that this chart was prepared by Mr. Sanford Evans, a statistician associated, I believe, with the grain trade, and he alone is responsible for the chart.
Who, Mr. Evans?

That is my understanding, and I do not think I am doing an injustice to Mr. Evans in so saying. I desire to make it as clear as I possibly can that as far as Sir Josiah Stamp is concerned I believe he left the country before the final printing of the report
lMr. I. A. Mackenzie.]
was complete, and so could not have had knowledge of it. As every hon. member knows, he was in rather a hurry to leave the country. In studying the report I noticed among other things that there were certain discrepancies in this chart. I will not say that I have had either the time or the material with which to make a critical examination of the report, but I did take some time to look into it. I do not think Mr. Evans has been fair in not allowing the cooperative prices to include that which is deducted for elevator and certain other charges, amounting roughly to three cents. To my mind that is not a fair treatment of the subject. I do not think I can make it any clearer to the committee that the government is not responsible for this or any other portion of the report. We accepted the report as it was submitted to us, and as far as I know this particular chart was inserted by Mr. Sanford Evans and by no one else. The government is not sanctioning the further circulation of the report containing that chart, believing the chart not to be an official part of the report.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has just made the statement that Sir Josiah Stamp left the country rather hurriedly and probably did not see the report when completed. On May 14 I asked the following question:
Some ten days ago I asked the Prime Minister when we might expect the tabling of the Stamp report. The Prime Minister replied on that occasion that it would be some ten days thence, but probably he would make a statement prior to that time. I wonder if he is now in a position to make that statement.
The Prime Minister made the following reply:
The Stamp report will be tabled just as soon as a cable is received from Sir Josiah Stamp. I had prepared a precis of the report, but it was thought undesirable to present it to the house until Sir Josiah Stamp had himself seen the final proof of the report which he had completed before he left America.
According to the reply made by the Prime Minister we must assume that the appendix was attached to the report when seen by Sir Josiah Stamp in its final form.

I do not think the hon. member desires to be unfair either to Sir Josiah Stamp or to the government. The report as it is in my hand is a bound report, and I think that any hon. member opposite who has had to do with the printing of reports knows that what is done is to send the typewritten sheets to the printer. These typewritten sheets are submitted to the author of the report but frequently the complete compilation is not seen by him. I cannot

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
understand why there should be any question about this matter; it is quite obvious that this particular diagram was inserted after the report was printed.
After it was printed?
Any hon. member who has knowledge of printing will see that.
That makes it worse.
It may make it worse, but I am just drawing that to the attention of the committee. I direct the attention of the committee to the physical conditions surrounding this diagram.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to point out to my hon. friend that this chart is affixed to the report in exactly the same manner as the other authentic charts to which I referred. When this report was received, after it had been perused by Sir Josiah Stamp in England, was it read by the minister or any other member of the government before it was printed, and who authorized the printing of the said report?

I am not seeking to evade responsibility, but the fact is that the Sir Josiah Stamp commission was appointed at the instance of the government as a whole, on the diredt authority of the Prime Minister speaking for the government. That is indicated in the order of reference. Neither the Department of Trade and Commerce nor its officials had anything to do with the preparation of the report.
Did the minister or did the Prime Minister read the report of Sir Josiah Stamp before it was printed and distributed in its present form?
The first time I saw the report was in blue book form, and I read it then very carefully and with great interest.
I accept the minister's assurance in that regard. Did the Prime Minister peruse this report after it had been received from Sir Josiah Stamp?

I do not know.
Mr. MaoINNJS:	I think the committee
should endeavour to get to the heart of this matter. As I understand it, the government appointed a commission to bring out certain facts with regard to a certain matter. If deductions had been made from the report, or if it had been mutilated in any way, then the governmenlt would have had an obvious duty to perform to find out who mutilated the report. In this instance, additions have been made to the report and the question is: What
is the government going to do with the members of the commission, or what action is it going to take against them for making an addition to the report? That is the thing in a nutshell.	[DOT]
My hon. friends across (the way seem to be rather fretful, but I desire to ask-
Order.

There are some seventeen ministers in the present cabinet, and I desire to ask if any of those hon. ministers perused this report before it was printed. Did the hon. Minister of Railways peruse this report before it was printed? Did my hon. friend the Postmaster General peruse this report before it was printed?
Hear, hear.
Did the Minister of National Defence peruse this report? Did the Minister of the Interior peruse this report?
Name every one of them.

Did the
Minister of Agriculture, who is most concerned, peruse this report?
Hear, hear.
Mr. Chairman, I can stand here until midnight.
Order.

I see my very attentive friend the Minister of Public Works in the chamber. Did he peruse the report? I see the Minister of Marine in hi3 seat. Did he peruse the report? This is a government, the largest in point of numbers and the most extravagant that we have ever had in Canada. I wish to assure the committee that this is one of the most flagrant breaches of parliamentary etiquette that parliament has ever witnessed. This is nothing but a false report. I deliberately, on my responsibility as a member, term it a false report, presented to parliament on the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he assumes the responsibility, or, if he does not, then on the authority of the Prime Minister of Canada.
As the hon. member for Vancouver South has just said, if any departmental official or member of a commission mutilated a government document presented to parliament, it would be a most serious offence. In this case we have an equally serious offence: we have an un-authorized exhibit appendix XII, as regards which no one knows whence it came,
3052	COMMONS
Supply-Royal Grain Commission
who put it there or who printed it. The minister of the crown who was responsible did not read the report; the Prime Minister did not read it, or, if he did read it, he is guilty of negligence irP permitting the insertion of this appendix.

Did my hon. friend
read it himself?

Yes, I
did; and I understood it, which is possibly more than my friend could do. We have before us to-day a false report entitled "report of the commission to inquire into trading in grain futures", a commission presided over by one of the most distinguished economists in Great Britain, brought to Canada for this very purpose. His reputation is absolutely endangered, I believe in my heart of hearts without his knowledge, throughout this dominion by the addition to this report of a spurious document not authorized or recognized by any well known body of public opinion in Canada. Not a single minister of the crown, not even the Prime Minister, has assumed responsibility for appendix XII, and I think the people of western Canada who are mostly concerned with this report are entitled to an explanation as to who is responsible for mutilating it in this unwarranted manner.
I notice the Minister of Trade and Commerce denies all responsibility with respect to this report. Am I to understand that such is the case?
No; my hon. friend must not put words into my mouth.
I am not trying to do so.
I am quite sure my hon. friend is too honourable to do that.
I hope so.

I have repeatedly stated
to-night, and I should not have to repeat again, that this is the report of Sir Josiah Stamp which the present government received as a most excellent presentation of the subject upon which the commission sat. The government itself, that is, the Prime Minister, myself and other members of the cabinet, in so far as their attention was drawn to the report, noted the discrepancy regarding this chart. Surely I have made it clear to the committee that the government does not condone, does not excuse, the presence of this chart in the report, and to show its good faith in the matter, as soon as this chart was discovered, the government stopped further circulation

of the report with this chart attached. I want hon. gentlemen opposite to appreciate the fact that we tabled the report in perfect good faith, fully believing that it contained a report in toto, approved and sanctioned by the commission as a whole; but as soon as we discovered this particular chart, as regards which I say very frankly I think there are justifiable grounds for complaint-I myself drew attention to it as soon as I had an opportunity to read and study the report-we stopped the further circulation of the report with this chart attached. I have explained the situation as clearly as I can to the committee, and I cannot understand why the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the member for Melville and others should insist upon accusing the government of seeking to hide or to condone something. I should be glad if the hon. member for Quebec East, who in his capacity previously as Minister of Justice used frequently to make such excellent expositions, would draft some form in which I could make this point quite clear, I am sure he understands it. I have not the slightest objection to my hon. friends opposite condemning this chart as strongly as they feel inclined, but I do not want them to saddle the government with the responsibility of it.
Has Mr. Sanford Evans been paid any remuneration for this work, or has he been promised anything by the government?

I do not know. I presume the commission were paid their expenses and perhaps certain remuneration was given to the commissioners other than Sir Josiah Stamp, who. I am proud to say, very generously gave his time without charge, feeling that he was rendering a service to this country. Again I take the opportunity to commend the exemplary manner in which he discharged his duty.
How much was paid to Mr. Sanford Evans for his services?

I do not know. The

A few moments ago the minister rose to correct me when I inferred from his remarks that the government

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
was not responsible. He rose and indicated that the government was responsible. Is that right?
My hon. friend is not trying to understand me.
I am. If he denies that they are not responsible, then we must assume that they are responsible.
