The minister did not make himself clear.

In so far as the receiving of this report from Sir Josiah Stamp and the commission over which he presided is concerned, we take full responsibility of presenting it to parliament as his report; but after the report was tabled it was discovered by the Prime Minister and myself, as members of the government, that a certain chart referred to as appendix XII was attached to the report, apparently without warrant. We have stopped the further circulation of the report with that chart in it, and we do not assume responsibility in any way for chart No. XII.
Does the minister mean to say that the government incurs no responsibility whatever for not reading a report before tabling and distributing it?

My right hon. friend is well enough acquainted with the procedure of government and the work that governments have to do to know that a government receives a report in perfect good faith from a commission. I ask him now in fairness to the government: Had he received the report in the form in which we have it at present, including this chart, is there any likelihood of discovering the fact that this particular chart was not referred to in the report?

I cannot conceive of a report being received by the Prime Minister without his reading it himself or at least referring it to one of his colleagues, and requesting him to read it through and advise him upon it before having it printed and laid on the table of the house and made available for distribution. The very first obligation upon a government, it seems to me, is to read a report that is made to it. The next is to decide whether it will publish the report, and the third is to decide whether it will distribute it. But the government appeare to have published and distributed the
report without ever having first read it to see whether or not it should be published in whole or in part.

The right hon. gentleman is not correct. The report was received and was read. As far as this particular chart is concerned, I submit that unless it is examined very carefully for the mistakes which we will all now admit it contains, it is very difficult to discover or recognize them. I read this report over with great care and I will admit that I did not at the first reading notice the inaccuracies in this chart, and I question if there are very many who would have noticed them unless they studied the chart with particular care. The insertion of that chart in the report appears to have been done without the knowledge of Sir Josiah Stamp or the authority of the commission as a whole. I am not excusing it, I am not in any sense justifying it. The fact is that it was there, and when it was discovered we stopped it.

The mistake
my hon. friend is making is in trying to excuse the government for an oversight of which ho ought frankly to admit the government was guilty.

Did the government
notice that this appendix was attached to the report prior to June 19, when the hon. member for Humboldt asked the Prime Minister a question regarding the report? Is that the first time the matter was drawn to their attention? Some members of this house have been rather annoyed at the insistence of some of us in asking for the tabling of this report. Here is the reason why we have been asking the Prime Minister from time to time when we could expect the report to be tabled. That is why I asked the Prime Minister today, on the orders of the day, if there would be a time set apart for the discussion of the Stamp report. We wanted to get at the facts of this matter. The first indication we had from the government that they had any knowledge of this appendix being attached to the report, which they now admit should not have been there, was on June 19, when the hon. member for Humboldt asked the Prime Minister a question which will be found on page 2812 of Hansard. Had the government any knowledge of the appendix being there prior to that date?

I think it was a few days prior to that. It was obvious that the Prime Minister was aware of the circumstance when the question was asked, so it would be absurd

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
to say that he had no knowledge of it prior to that time. Just what day or hour or place it was, I do not know.

I am not very anxious
about the hour. But will not the hon. gentleman himself admit that if a minister had announced, when the government became aware of the inclusion of this appendix in the report that it was there without the knowledge of the commission, this thing would never have happened? Just how would the matter have gone had it not been for the opposition put up by those not immediately interested in the grain trade so far as Winnipeg is concerned?
It would not have gone any distance.
Was it not Chief Justice Brown who drew the attention of the government to this appendix?

I do not think so. I think the attention of the Prime Minister was first drawn to it so far as I recall-I am speaking now without absolute knowledge-by Mr. Travers Sweatman, counsel to the commission.

Has the government taken any steps to send out circulars to those into whose hands this pamphlet has been placed, to correct the wrong impression which they may have received? Have they taken any steps whatever?
Not that I know of.
Do they propose to do so?

I should be surprised if their attention was not drawn to it by the discussion in the house to-night. I think my hon. friends will agree with me that they have done noble work to-night in the defence of the liberties of the country by crossquestioning and pillorying me rather viciously. I have no objections to it; I rather enjoy it, but I am very sorry indeed, I say so frankly, that this appendix was attached to the report. In so far as any injustice has been done, it is regrettable, but I am quite certain of this, that with such energetic defenders as we have witnessed among the opposition to-night, and with their brilliancy of presentation, the derelictions of whomsoever may be responsible will be plainly put before the people of this country, and the government, of course, patiently and with all due forbearance, will have to take its medicine.
It will have to have its appendix out.
I had mine carved out a while ago.
Does not my hon. friend now admit that this is a case where the government delayed too long in performing a very necessary operation upon the appendix?
Judging from the proceedings to-night, I would say that the appendix had burst.

The appendix has not quite burst yet. I was going to ask if the government had pursued the usual practice,, when a report is received, of having a minister or some of the officials of the department peruse it very carefully, including all the appendices, no matter how many in number.

My hon. friend the other night used an expression that touched me very deeply. It was on a Friday night, and he referred to standing on the verge of Jordan looking across to the other side. It so impressed me that I took this report home and spent nearly all the next Sunday reading it.
It is not the river Jordan that you are nearest to, but I fear the river Styx.
I am a pretty good paddler, and will paddle my way across.

My hon. friend is
evading my question. Did the officials of the department, or anybody, carefully peruse all these documents in the usual way that any hobo government would do before the report was published? I know that I cannot get anything to the printer until it had been gone over a good many times so see that everything was right, and surely a public document of this character prepared by a recognized economist from Great Britain should have been done justice to. It should have been carefully scrutinized before it was ever sent to the printer, but apparently that was neglected. Am I wrong in that?

I will speak on behalf
of my own department. There is no official in my department who was culpable in any respect.

There is something wrong. I remember two years ago that when the Brown commission was investigating the grain question the farmers in dozens recommended that the whole grain problem be put into the hands of the Department of Agriculture, like all other agricultural matters and

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
products. There was no reason, they said, why grain should come under the Department of Trade and Commerce any more than live stock, and they recommended strongly that the Department of Agriculture should take it over. That was going to be rather embarrassing for certain gentlemen at that time to recommend, but now it can be recommended with more freedom. Now that we see how this matter is handled by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and now that we have a real Minister of Agriculture- accent on " real "-why cannot this grain question be handed over to the Department of Agriculture?
Evidently there was no particular supervision of this report before it was printed. I do not think I have ever heard of a report of a commission being brought down with this kind of blunder in it. Of course it is not unusual for this government to commit blunders. Here we have an object lesson of just what has been happening all over the world where any member of this government has gone during the last nine months, whether to Rome, or London, or Belfast, or Jericho, in connection with selling wheat. They have stumbled and blundered every time where wheat was concerned. I will tell you how I think this appendix got in here. I do not think any member of the government appreciated the significance of this appendix or what it meant. I am going to absolve them of any deliberate intention of putting it in there although it is difficult to imagine such simplicity. The chart reached the report, however, and stupid as this government is on grain questions, the significance of the chart was not recognized.
Order.

Wh'o says "order''? Now my hon. friend would like to transfer some of the responsibility to one particular member of the commission, William Sanford Evans. There can be no more individual responsibility in a commission than there can be individual responsibility in a government. The government is an entity and so was the commission.
A nonentity.

No member of the commission is a nonentity, and I must say that William Sanford Evans is technically at least no more responsible than is Sir Josiah Stamp or Mr. Justice Brown. Hon. members may try to dismember them, take their appendices out or anything they like, but they simply cannot make the commission anything but an entity. If Mr. William Sanford Evans
was the genius who did the trick, the whole commission is responsible-that is the unfortunate fact-just as this whole government is responsible for the costly blunder which has been made and the injustice which has been done to a great organization which has held the admiration of the cooperative world, and which to-day is staggering under the prevailing economic conditions. Under these circumstances this government has dealt a solar plexus blow-unwittingly if you like-but at the same time its objective seems to be while professing friendship to put the organization out of business. The Minister of Agriculture stated in his famous speech that when we learn what the government is doing for the wheat pool we will blush for shame. Well, whose turn is it to blush for shame now? The government professedly the friend of the pool, gives it a diabolical stab in the back which pretty nearly puts it out of business. I am sure we have never witnessed such extraordinary action before.
The Stamp commission was heralded throughout Canada as a real crackerjack commission; it was expected it would bring in a crackerjack report and that the report would be filed before a crackerjack government. Are we labouring under a delusion? Must we change our ideas and admit that we were then only in a trance, only in a dream? Must we consider that the whole thing is up in the air so far as all these crackerjack propositions are concerned?

Did the cabinet in
council ever examine or discuss this appendix?
As any hon. member acquainted with the constitution must know, it is not customary to discuss in the house what happened in council.
If the minister wishes to give that answer, well and good.

Does not the minister think that once the cabinet discovered an appendix which improperly appeared in the report it was the duty of the government immediately to disclose that fact to parliament and to the country?

I think it was disclosed
very shortly afterwards.

Only
when the information was dragged out.

not "dragged out". A very direct and courteous answer was given by the Prime Minister to the question asked. I am sure the answer was not "dragged out", in any sense of the term.

How long was that after the mistake was discovered?

I told one of my hon. friend's colleagues no more than a minute ago that I did not know. I do know, however, that the Prime Minister had knowledge of it as I had, and that the circulation of the report with the appendix in it has been stopped.

Was it not the duty of the Prime Minister, as soon as the discovery was made, to make an immediate pronouncement to parliament? The announcement was not made to parliament *until a question was asked by the hon. member for Humboldt. According to the statement of the minister, however, he and the Prime Minister knew the fact some considerable time before the question was asked in the house. My suggestion is that it was the duty of the government immediately the mistake was discovered to make an announcement both to parliament and to the country so that nobody would be misled by the report.

The moment I saw the appendix to which so much exception has been taken to-night I sought the opinion of one of the leading economists in our western university. At my request he made an analysis of the appendix. As an example of vicious propaganda, unjustifiable and gross misrepresentation this appendix stands almost without peer. The young gentleman who made the analysis had nothing to gain by the advice he gave me, yet he told me that the appendix contains no less than nine statistical errors. I am sure it could not have been the product of a mind like that of Sir Josiah Stamp or that of Mr. William Sanford Evans. If the latter named gentleman is responsible for this report, he can never again raise his head as an economist in Canada.

When the Prime Minister replied to the question of the hon. member for Humboldt, he said:
My attention has been drawn to the matter. As I understand it, the appendix was an exhibit filed with the commission.
Now we are told that is not so.
My hon. friend has not been told that.

If it was an exhibit, Sir Josiah Stamp would be aware of the fact that the appendix is in there, and I agree with 
my hon. friend from Bow River; I do not think Sir Josiah Stamp knows anything about it.

If my hon. friend will read Hansard to-morrow he will see that on at least five occasions to-night I have stated that appendix XII, chart No. 10, obviously was a graph tabled with the commission by Mr. William Sanford Evans.

There i3 not another appendix in the report which does not state by whom and when it was filed. If appendix No. XH was filed there should be some indication of that in the report. Although I have read the report many times, I have found no mention therein of appendix XII.
No?
Or of who filed it, or when was it tabled.
We agree on that.

The question by the hon. member for Humboldt, and the reply given by the Prime Minister, were as follows:

Bight Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister): My attention has been drawn to the matter. As I understand it, the appendix was an exhibit filed with the commission, and it was to be included in the report of the commission, but there is upon that appendix some printing which draws inferences that may or may not have been warranted, and that should not have been there. The diagram itself is not a matter of great importance; the objectionable feature is the printing that was put on it, I think by the grain exchange, in connection with certain propaganda, and it should not have been put upon the copy that was printed. That is my understanding of the situation. Either it can he taken from the report, or if any reprints of the report are made, that printing will not appear upon the appendix.
So now we must assume that it is only since June 19 that the government deleted from this report the appendix of which we complain, because in no uncertain words the Prime Minister says that it can be taken from the report or that if any reprints of the report are made the appendix will not appear therein. So that up until June 19 these reports have been printed and sent out as they appear tonight, and only those sent out since June 19 will be without the appendix.
he not give them any chance to reply to it? Did he say, "Sanford Evans put this in and you will have to take your medicine?"

I cannot say.

It is like Topsy, it just growed up. The more one studies this matter the more serious it becomes. Here is the last edition of the report. The insertion of this appendix is a fitting climax to the whole record of the government in connection with the killing of the wheat pool. We know that as a result of the trip of the Prime Minister and his colleagues to Britain Mr. John McFarland was appointed as the salesman for the wheat pool. We know also that twenty-seven of the pool agencies have been withdrawn in Britain and on the continent. We know further, from the reports we have obtained, not only from Britain but, as well, from France, Italy and Spain, that the withdrawal of these wheat pool agencies has had a serious effect on the price which was obtained for the wheat that was held and marketed formerly by the pool. So that the more we study this whole thing-unless we get some further insight from members of the government into what has been done-the more we are forced to the conclusion that, as I have said, the insertion of this appendix is a fitting climax to the whole record of the government in regard to the wheat pool.

I should like to ask if it is not true that the research council have been working in conjunction with the scientists of the nickel companies in seeking a method by which commercial uses could be made of the products which hitherto not only have been wasted 'but have made the securing of the precious metals from the ores more difficult than otherwise would be the case. I am aware that as a result of what has been done in that direction a substantial amount of wealth is being secured from a product contained in the ores extracted in northern Ontario which formerly was not only wasted but which formed a very serious menace to the whole countryside because of the sulphur fumes which were being thrown off and which spoiled the whole district. I understand that this product now has a valuable commercial use.
Following that, may I say that if my information is correct the experts of these companies, in association with the national research council, are endeavouring to find a means by which they can also extract the iron content of these ores. If they are successful this will mean a tremendous addition to the national wealth of this country, because this is what is taking place: By the process of smelting they are wasting 53 per cent of the metal content of the ores taken from some of the mines, because they have not reached the point as yet where they can extract both the base and precious metals from the same ores. They are working on it all the time, however, and they have succeeded in devising a method by which the sulphuric content can be made of commercial value to a very large degree, instead of being a waste and a menace, which it has been ever since these mines were put in operation. My information is that they have been and Still are working with the national research council, and are getting very valuable assistance from the council.

I think my hon. friend was really good enough to answer his own questions. I have been following his observations, and what he says is quite true. Professor Haultain and Doctor Moore and others have been working on these complex problems having to do with the treatment of ores in Ontario and other parts of the country, and I understand they are cooperating in the solution of these problems.

I just want to say to the minister that I very much approve of this vote. I was interested to read an article in the paper recently stating that research was being carried on with regard to the possibility of finding other uses for wheat, and I should like to ask if any success has been attained as yet.

They are working on that question in the laboratories here, and I understand the same research is being carried out in Germany and other countries. I think the subject is so much in its infancy that little can be said with regard to the progress made.

I should like to
draw the attention of the minister to the tendency of the national research council, in its desire to consolidate research work, to attempt to absorb non-absorbable research work which does not lend itself to other than agricultural activity. I refer more particularly to a seed laboratory for the seed branch of the Department of Agriculture, which is very much required at the present time. This work is scattered around the city to-day, as it has been for the last quarter of a century, and the opinion has been expressed that it should be attached to the new research building. A seed laboratory is a peculiar and special kind of laboratory. It requires special light for the purpose of analyzing and classifying seeds. They must be subjected to an analytical examination having regard to purity of variety, freedom from weed seed and so on, which requires an exceedingly good northern light exposure. In addition, several acres of land close to the building are required in order to conduct the necessary growing experiments having to do with the germinating properties, purity of variety of the seeds. I wish my hon friend to take note of that, because a seed laboratory associated with the present new research building, no matter how fine it may be, would be entirely unsuited for the work. The light facilities must be prepared when the building is being erected, and in addition there would be the lack of the
necessary land upon which to conduct growing experiments already mentioned. A seed laboratory requires a separate building with proper light, and a considerable amount of land upon which to conduct the necessary field tests.

How can the department ascertain what good certain advertising does, in the case of Canadian advertising such as the minister has spoken of? Can the minister tell us how much was spent in Great Britain last year?

The minister

Speaking offhand, I think about $95,000. I have not the exact figures, but that . is approximate.

I think not.
Will the minister tell us how much it cost to print "My Creed," and how many copies were printed.

No, copies. And we have demands for at least 100,000 more, if we print more. There is a wide demand for them. The cost of printing was $7,300.60.

Does not my

"My Creed" and is printed on cardboard. It is highly illuminated, bearing the coats of arms of the dominion and of all the provinces, with maple leaves, roses-

Very nicely done, I
thought.
And thistles-
Thorns, you mean.
I think it is very good.

Yes, but there are many things very much better. My hon. friend might take any chapter from the scriptures and print it, and it would be much truer and better than anything he has here. But the question is, what justification has the government for using the taxes of the people at the present time for this kind of thing? That is the point. Does the minister justify the use of public money for such a thing? Here is a copy of the document. As the committee will see, it is illuminated with all the colours of the rainbow and is highly decorated. How does the minister justify the use of public money for the distribution by the government of Canada of this sort of thing by the hundreds of thousands, or whatever the number is that he has indicated?
I stated a moment ago that had I anticipated reaching this item I would have brought with me the letters. I justify this in two ways: first, the sentiments I think are well worthy of support.
We are not paying for sentiments during these hard times.
A little sentiment is a very useful thing, and a little hope and confidence in one's country is very desirable.
Under this government?
That is my first justification. My second justification is that there was an overwhelming demand by the. public for this creed.
It is a pretty picture.

I will refer in a moment to the pretty picture. The first publication was made in newspaper form with an invitation attached for the purpose of ascertaining its effect. The responses to that inquiry were so overwhelming that I think I am justified in saying it was a complete success. We could distribute to-day at least 100,000; we have received requests from all over Canada and from every class of people. Hundreds have been distributed in northern Ontario, in the province of Quebec and in the prairie priv-inces. In many cases school inspectors upon seeing the creed have written in and asked
for a supply for distribution in the schools, claiming that it had a good educational value, and that the sentiments contained therein were such as should be disseminated as widely as possible. Whatever may be the opinion of the right hon. gentleman, I have no apologies to make for this effort; I think it has been wholly and amply justified.
A rather slighting remark was made a moment ago about the coloured picture, but I want to say that the lithographing or printing of this creed is a credit to the printing art of Canada. The design was not conceived by myself, but I think it is one which might appeal to the educative instincts of the people. It sets forth the various provincial coats of arms as well as the dominion coat of arms. It is open to my right hon. friend to laugh at it and make fun of it; I accord to him that privilege, if he desires to use it, but it has grown out of a response which was beyond our anticipation and we feel that we have done a very good piece of work in sending that creed throughout Canada. There was no thought of partisanship in the issue of that creed; if my right hon. friend has that in his mind I can assure him there was nothing of the sort.

Mr. Chairman, even if the Minister of Trade and Commerce can produce a whole file of recommendations, I do not think it would alter the situation. It would be quite, easy to find 100,000 people who would be glad to make application for creeds damning the present government from A to Z. They could be placed in every post office throughout Canada; I know that every farmer in the west would be glad to have an illuminated creed of that sort. It is ridiculous to think that public money should be spent in this fashion. The leader of the opposition has said it was a waste of public money; I would not say it is a "waste" of public money, but I say it is a misuse of public money.
It is both.

Both, if the right hon. gentleman likes, but it is much more serious to misuse public money than it is to waste it. Under the guise of government advertising, the government has carried on a definite political compaign.
It is political propaganda.

It has enunciated certain political creeds which are believed in by one. party in this country but are not believed in by the other parties. It has enunciated certain economic doctrinog which are
Supply-Trade and Commerce

false in almost every line and which are condemned by nearly all the leading economists in Canada and throughout the world. We who are responsible in this committee for the use of public money have a right to protest against a campaign of that kind. I hold in my hands a reproduction of one of these letters. I do not know how many of them have been published, but this particular one is directed to the wage earners of Canada. It is entitled "Don't be penny wise pound foolish!'' In the most approved style it attempts to persuade the consumer, especially the wage earning consumer, that it is absolute folly for him to buy goods which are not produced in Canada.
Hear, hear.
Hon. gentlemen say "hear, hear"; they have a right to their opinions-
They do not know any better.

I do not object to hon. gentlemen holding certain opinions, but I have the right to mine, and I object to public money being used to propagate their Opinions. That is where the trouble lies. I should like to read a few sentences from this letter which attempts to dissuade the people of Canada from buying foreign made articles. The letter reads:
Like as not the foreign producer, whom you would be helping out of a jam if you purchased his bargain, has a production cost that is far below the Canadian cost of producing the same article.
There is a statement which has nothing behind it. I could just as easily say: Like as not, the Canadian cost is lower than that of the foreign cost and therefore we are putting money into the hands of the manufacturer without receiving anything back. That was amply shown by the hon. member for Beauharnois who outlined the tremendous profits made by the textile corporations.
If the Canadian cost is less than the foreign cost, the goods would not be imported.

That may or may not be the case; even the hon. members are endeavouring to delude themselves on matters of this kind. The letter continues:
And if you were to institute inquiries with a view to finding out why his production cost was so much lower, like as not you would find it was because he was paying his employees rates of wages that were away below the scale paid to similar work in this country.

Hon. members who have compared the wages paid in the United States with those paid in Canada have found that very frequently the wages in this country are much lower than those paid in the United States. Here we have an absolute misstatement of the situation. Assistance is given to the Canadian manufacturer who is paying low wages. The letter continues:
In that event, it would be reasonably safe to assume that a much lower standard of living prevails among the workers in his country than prevails here.
For all we know, the standard of living in other countries may be much higher than in Canada. The letter continues:
Possibly he requires his employees to work longer hours than is customary in Canada.
In many cases, the hours in other countries are shorter than those prevailing in Canada. The fact that an article is made in a foreign country does not mean that the hours worked were longer, or that lower wages were paid. And again:
Possibly the laws of his country are not as strict as they are here regarding the employment of child labour.
Any hon. member who has read the reports of the Department of Labour in connection with child labour must be shocked at the large number of children employed in industry in Canada. There are proportionately twice as many as in the United States. These are figures that are given by our own Department of Labour, yet in this advertisement all that is slurred over and we are led to believe that we have less child labour in this country than elsewhere, which is not true. The article continues:
Possibly he is not taxed, as Canadian manufacturers' are taxed, to ensure compensation on a reasonable scale being paid his workmen who suffer injury in the course of their employment.
Again let me say, when one looks at the reports of the International Labour Office and notes the large number of countries apart from Canada which have provisions for this very type of social legislation and notes how little of it we have in Canada, one realizes that this is pure bluff; there is nothing to it; it is misrepresentation. Yet this is being put over in the name of the government of this country. I quote further:
Possibly he is not required to maintain his factory at anything like as high standards of ventilation, of sanitation, of heating, of lighting, of protection against fire and accident, as are in force in Canada.
In all these matters-hours of labour, rates of wages, standards of living, factory inspection, social legislation and industrial better-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ment work-Canada is much more advanced than most of the nations that make products similar to hers.
That is absolutely untrue, as is shown, again let me say, by the reports of the International Labour Office as well as other authoritative documents. Yet we have that propaganda put over, for what purposes? Simply to boost some Canadian manufacturers, and in order to lull us into a kind of false self-satisfaction with things in general in this country. The article continues:
The result is that Canadian wage earners are more fortunately circumstanced in almost every way, than are the wage earners in most other countries.
Is that true? When for years such large numbers left Canada to go to the United States, it did not look as if they were so much better off in this country than elsewhere. I quite admit that present conditions are as bad and probably worse in the United States. I continue reading:
Obviously they can only hope to retain those advantages as long as their employers, the manufacturers of Canada, are able to overcome in the domestic market the competition of foreign-made goods that are produced under longer working hours, lower wage scales, and lower standards of living.
Again a misstatement of the situation.
For should the time ever come when they can no longer compete, either their Canadian employees must agree to wage reductions and the loss of decent living conditions, or the manufacturers themselves must close up shop.
Surely there are enough men of the stamp of Sir Joseph Flavelle going around this country preaching lower wages and threatening employees without the government doing the same thing and paying $100,000 of the country's money to do it. The article proceeds :
You can see therefore what serious trouble these bargains in foreign-made goods may cause you-what serious trouble any foreign-made goods may cause you whether they be bargains or not-if you allow yourself to be persuaded into buying them.
What in the name of common sense is the use of our having a Department of Trade and Commerce, having our trade officials all over the world at great cost, and publishing all sorts of documents if we are going to cut off our trade with the rest of the world? I would say that the Department of Trade and Commerce might as well go out of business. The idea of actually spending these huge sums of money simply to instruct the people they must not buy foreign made goods when we all know quite well that unless we do buy foreign made goods, we can never send goods out of this country! That is the elementary 22110-195
economics of the situation and we are beclouding the whole issue by this so-called campaign. The article goes on:
Should you say there is nothing harmful in buying them once in a while, you will probably see nothing harmful in buying them every chance you get.
This simply means that we ought to take as part of our creed that we shall never buy any foreign goods. That is surely a reduetio ad absurdum.
And if you buy them every chance you get, you cannot blame others for doing the same thing. Once everybody in Canada starts doing it, you know what will happen!
I ask hon. gentlemen if all the clothing they wear is made out of wool manufactured in Canada. Do they never buy suits made out of the best English cloths?
What about their automobiles?

Yes; I fancy they
sometimes buy things that are made outside Canada. What about those articles that come under our ordinary diet in this country? Are we to be told that all our citrus fruits must be grown in Canada and that we must never stop to buy anything that is made or produced outside this country? The situation is ridiculous. The article winds up on this high moral plane:
So for the sake of a small immediate saving or merely to satisfy a passing whim, why run the risk of setting in train a movement that in a few years might easily prove your undoing! Wouldn't it be far better for you, and your family, and all your friends, to stand fast by the policy of buying "produced-in-Canada," as the surest means of protecting Canadian rates of wages and Canadian standards of living?
Following up this wonderful campaign, we find almost every province taking up the cry and we have in my own province a "Pro-duced-in-Manitoba" campaign. Our local manufacturers are protesting against anything being brought in from Ontario and Quebec because we want everything produced in Manitoba. Out in Saskatchewan they are insisting that all their beers must be produced in that province, and none of them in Alberta or Manitoba, and so the idea travels. Every word of this campaign, if it be true for the dominion, is equally true for the provinces; it is equally true for each little city across the country. I mention this only to show how absurd the whole thing is. Let me say again, standing in my place as representing one constituency in Canada, I protest against the misuse of public money in carrying on a party campaign of this kind.



Supply-Trade and Commerce

When these display cards were gotten out by the government as a beautiful exhibit of lithographing and the advertisements generally were published, I put some of the clippings away, but they became so numerous I was not able to keep track of them. They were nothing but campaign literature. During these hard times fine words and feathers may be all right, but they do not butter any parsnips, and they cost a lot of money. May I quote one part of the creed:
We have unbounded confidence in the ability of her people to excel in whatsoever they undertake.
Supposing we substitute the words "the present government" for the words "her people." Then it would read:
We have unbounded confidence in the ability of the present government to excel in whatsoever they undertake.
Well, have we? If my hon. friends opposite have a large quantity of these cards on hand I would recommend that they sell them quickly because the demand is going down rapidly and these cards will soon be at a tremendous discount. Therefore they should sell them quickly while the selling is good, because the exhibition that we had this evening in connection with the Stamp commission report will discount them still further. I think the whole propaganda is ridiculous and absurd; the government have not lived up to the stuff contained in this creed, much less to the realities of life. Whatever major task they have undertaken, failure has dogged their steps from early morning until dewy eve. Of course they have been able to tax us. They are whales' on protection, on looking after the manufacturer. They rushed to Ottawa to a special session, fell upon the necks of the manufacturers and met them more than half-way. They were prepared to do all and even more than the manufacturers wanted to be done or could think of asking for. They are a success in such matters as increasing the postage rates, cancelling the penny postage and imposing all these little annoying taxes; they are certainly whales at that; but a3 regards dealing with any major proposition confronting Canada at this time, nobody can deny that they have fallen down all along the line. Look at the Minister of Justice-the picture of despair. I heard him over the radio during the last election campaign and he gave the most effective speech and the most damaging to the Liberal cause that was given in that part of the country, and that is saying something because his colleague to his right (Mr. Stevens), whom I also heard, 
was no mean stump speaker. I certainly admired the ingenuity with which he twisted things. And the Prime Minister, well, he was simply magnificent as an orator over the radio. I remember the Minister of Justice over the radio was complaining about the mixing of wheat, and he asked why did we not fix it up quicker. But we havn't heard a peep out of him since then, but we will attend to that matter before the grain act vote is through. The Minister of Justice has been significantly quiet all this session. Why does he not get up and defend this propaganda? Surety he can defend it as well as he defended the economic conference in London. This government should be condemned up hill and down dale for putting this advertising stuff out. It is purely Conservative propaganda. If I were a Conservative I presume I would look upon it with more leniency, but let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that there are thousands and tens of thousands of Conservatives who condemn this kind of thing just as much as I do. As a matter of fact, the Conservatives in the west will soon be as scarce as hens' teeth. There will not be enough of them to say anything one way or the other about this propaganda. Who is murmuring over there? Why don't you get up and say something?
Why don't you say something yourself while you are up?

I am trying to
pretty hard. We have pretty nearly silenced the whole government to-night on every question that has been brought up. Perhaps my hon. friend was not in the house when we were discussing the Stamp report.
Yes, I was.

Well, if he did
not get enough then, he does not know when he has got enough and must have a hide like a rhinoceros.

I should like
to say a word as to one aspect in particular of what the government is doing by this propaganda. We hear a good deal from the Prime Minister and others about the desirability of people, to say nothing of the opposition, saying as little as possible about the existing unemployment and distress. Hon. members opposite are continually saying that we should soft-pedal on that sort of thing. Let me read what appears in the first letter which the Minister of Trade and Commerce sent out over his own signature. It is dated October 4, 1930, just when unemployment was beginning to get a little worse.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
This is what the government of Canada has been paying the press of Canada to publish far and wide from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Here is a paragraph by itself:
As you know, thousands upon thousands of your fellow-Canadians are out of work. Unemployment, always a serious problem when it occurs, is more serious than ever just now, not only because it has lasted so long and been so widespread, but because of the unusually large numbers who, by reason of it, are being forced to suffer real hardships.
There is a statement published as an advertisement in most of the papers of Canada by this government and paid for out of public money. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other members of the government how, in the face of that statement, they can justify the position they are taking to-day of having in this country no policy whatever on unemployment. They have advertised that the unemployment situation was bad, that thousands and thousands were out of work, that the situation was getting worse, with people forced to suffer real hardships. They have used public money to send that advertisement broadcast throughout the country, and yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself, who is asking us to pay for that kind of thing, told this house only a few evenings ago that it was too early even yet to look for any pronouncement from the government as to its policy on unemployment. He said that we might expect to get it at the end of the session. I say, Mr. Chairman, the government had better consider very seriously the effect of this kind of thing. This is the sort of thing that is causing the people of this country to feel a sense of outrage towards this government; this playing fast and loose with unemploj-ment for protectionist propaganda purposes, exploiting the sufferings of the unemployed to help specially protected interests. The minister seeks to justify this and to ask us to appropriate public money for such purposes; when, however, attention is drawn to the need of immediate action to relieve unemployment throughout the country, notwithstanding that the government itself has been advertising unemployment and the extent and the seriousness of it, the minister sits perfectly dumb. When he does speak he tells the house that we need not expect an announcement of the government's policy on unemployment until the end of the session. How does the minister justify out of taxation paying for the circulation of a statement of that kind? How can he justify the expenditure of public money in sending broadcast through the 22110-195J
press of this country a paragraph such as appears there?
It is justified in the remainder of the letter.

The remainder of the letter only makes the thing worse; for if the country were to follow out what is there suggested, business would become stagnant in no time. The letter from which I have quoted is dated October 4, 1930. Let me read the first paragraph of another letter, dated November 1, 1930, and remember that unemployment conditions have steadily become worse from October 4, 1930, up to the present time. On November 1, 1930, the minister issues a statement as follows:
Some day soon you will be called upon by a commercial traveller who is going to do his best to sell you some foreign-made goods.
And the rest of the article sets forth the reasons why that commercial traveller should, metaphorically speaking, be kicked out, why he should not be listened to, why no foreign made goods should be bought. This is from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the head of the department that exists for the purpose of extending our trade and furthering international trade. Read through the whole article, and there is no one but will be convinced that the whole purpose of all this propaganda is to restrict trade in the interest of a few specially protected concerns. Its whole purpose is to make anything in the nature of international trade impossible. What does that mean? These advertisements are being paid for by the people of the prairie provinces just as much as by the people of Ontario and Quebec, and I ask the minister what right he has to use the money of the people of Manitoba, Allberta and Saskatchewan to advise the people of Canada, regardless of the part in which they live, not to buy any imported goods.
No right whatever.

What right has he to advise the people of Canada in advertisements paid for out of their taxes, when labour conditions are getting worse and worse throughout the country, not to buy any imported goods, and then to attempt to support his statements by whole pages of economic fallacies? I shall not call them economic arguments; they are economic fallacies.

Would the right hon.
gentleman advise the people of this country to the contrary, to buy foreign made goods?

I would advise the people to expand trade all that they possibly can at this time, to make trade as

extensive as possible. I see the hour is just up, Mr. Chairman, but before sitting down I should like to repeat what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just said, that no government has the right to use public moneys to further party political propaganda, and every bit of this advertising from beginning to close is, first of all, an effort to further propaganda in what it puts forth in the advertisements themselves, and in the second place to bring if possible the press of the country, through advertisements of this kind, under an obligation to the ministry for the advertising which they are being given in this way.
